web_evidence.title: Black and Blue Excerpt: Read free excerpt of Black and Blue by Anna Quindlen
web_evidence.note: A sustained nine-page promotional excerpt begins with Fran recounting her abuse as 'I' and continues in first-person narration; the page supplies an explicit copyright and promotional-use notice.

web_evidence.title: Review of Black and Blue
web_evidence.note: Frank L. Fennell's 1998 review, originally published in America, explicitly identifies the novel as Fran Benedetto's first-person narrative and discusses her controlling voice and the epilogue.

web_evidence.title: Black and Blue
web_evidence.note: Laura Green's contemporary review explicitly calls Fran the narrator and describes the novel's controlling voice as first person.

web_evidence.title: Black and Blue: A Novel
web_evidence.note: Google Books identifies the Random House edition and displays first-person passages from pages 1 and 8, corroborating the opening excerpt.

search_log: Searched "Anna Quindlen Black and Blue novel excerpt first chapter narrator first person" and located the sustained BookBrowse promotional excerpt, Google Books passages, and contemporary reviews.
Searched "Black and Blue Anna Quindlen point of view first person narrator" and opened explicit whole-book descriptions from America/eNotes, Salon, and BookRags.

Searched "Black and Blue Quindlen first-person narrative epilogue", "alternating point of view", and "diary narrator"; found confirmation of Fran's continuing narratorial voice and no evidence of sustained narration in another person.

Searched Penguin Random House, Random House, Google Books, Open Library, and Internet Archive; the publisher page verified the edition and offered a sample control, but its visible synopsis was not itself person evidence.
person_note: The event quotations repeatedly expose Fran/Beth as a participating 'I' narrator, while the lone sustained third-person-looking quotation merely describes Robert and remains compatible with her first-person account. Dialogue and universal gnomic uses of 'you' are local or nondiagnostic. A sustained authorized promotional opening and Google Books passages agree with two independent contemporary whole-book reviews explicitly identifying Fran's first-person narrative; targeted searches found no alternating-person structure. The only scope limitation is that the directly accessible prose excerpts cover the opening, but the whole-book reviews, including discussion of the epilogue, resolve that limitation.
